subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Availability: Easy to Recall Feels Common
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Availability: Easy to Recall Feels Common.

hook.text: Are there more words starting with 'K' or with 'K' as the third letter? Most say first. They're wrong.

buildup.text: Words starting with K come to mind faster. We mistake ease of recall for actual frequency.

discovery.text: Availability heuristic: we judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind.

twist.text: Plane crashes are vivid and memorable. Car crashes aren't. We fear flying more, but driving kills more.

climax.text: Media coverage, personal experience, and emotion all boost availability, warping our risk estimates.

punchline.text: Easy to remember doesn't mean likely to happen.

quiz.question: What does the availability heuristic cause?
options: We judge frequency by how easily examples come to mind
We always rely on statistical data

details.summary: The availability heuristic judges the frequency or probability of events by how easily examples come to mind. Dramatic, recent, or emotionally vivid events are recalled more easily and therefore judged as more common than mundane but statistically frequent events.
details.whyItMatters: The availability heuristic explains why people fear plane crashes more than car accidents, why recent news events dominate risk perception, and why vivid personal experiences outweigh statistical information in decision-making.
takeaways: Ease of recall substitutes for actual frequency in probability judgments
Media coverage amplifies perceived frequency of dramatic events
Personal experience with an event makes it feel more common than statistics suggest

faq.question: Why does the availability heuristic lead to poor risk assessment?
faq.answer: Because dramatic, newsworthy events are easy to recall, they are judged as more common and dangerous. Plane crashes, shark attacks, and terrorism get outsized fear despite being statistically rare, while common killers like heart disease receive less worry because they are less vivid.

faq.question: How can you correct for availability bias in your own thinking?
faq.answer: Check your intuitions against base rate statistics. If you feel something is common or likely, look up the actual frequency. Ask whether your estimate is driven by recent news or vivid memories rather than representative data.
